5: (1) One who cooks on Shabbos — {or who performed one of the other melachos (Tur)} — intentionally (b'meizid): it is forbidden to him forever, and for others it is permitted immediately after Shabbos. Unintentionally (b'shogeg): it is forbidden that day even for others, and in the evening it is permitted even for him immediately. {And if he told a non-Jew to perform a melacha on Shabbos, see above siman 307 seif 20.}
8: (1) 'Permitted immediately after Shabbos' — for we only require b'chedi she'ya'asu for a melacha performed by a non-Jew on behalf of a Jew, since it is light in his eyes and he may come to do so again. But something a Jew does with his own hands, there is certainly no concern that he will come to cook outright.
11: (1) 'Forbidden to him forever' — it is implied from the Rashba siman 175 that the pot is also forbidden.
13: (3) 'B'shogeg' — one who acted on the instruction of a sage is considered shogeg, and the same applies to one who forgot [so it is in the Radbaz, Beis 26, part 2].
15: (2) 'Permitted immediately after Motzei Shabbos' — specifically when a non-Jew performs the act do we require b'chedi she'ya'asu, since we fear he may tell him to do it again, but a Jew will not listen to him — Tosafos Chullin 15. And if Motzei Shabbos was Yom Tov it is forbidden, for Shabbos does not prepare for Yom Tov [Likkutei Mahariv siman 2]. And if that item became mixed with others, see the Magen Avraham.
17: (3) 'B'shogeg' — if he acted on the instruction of a sage he is considered shogeg, and the same applies to one who forgot — Knesset HaGedolah, Radbaz.
20: (1) Seif 1, 'One who cooks on Shabbos, etc.' — the Shulchan Aruch ruled like R' Yehuda and not R' Meir, because the unattributed ruling in Chullin follows his view. But Tosafos and those who agree with them ruled like R' Meir, and their proof is very clear. And what they wrote — that the unattributed ruling in Chullin follows R' Yehuda — this does not necessarily hold, since the unattributed ruling in chapter 2 of Terumos follows R' Meir, and likewise the sugya at the beginning of chapter 3 of Shabbos. And we rule like R' Yochanan who holds the halacha follows R' Yehuda.
22: (3) 'Immediately' — not like Rashi in Chullin 15a, nor the Baal HaMaor, who explained that b'chedi she'ya'asu is required; Tosafos in the third chapter of Yom Tov disagrees with them and holds that we rule like R' Shimon that muktzeh does not apply, and here there is a distinction between shogeg and meizid.
25: 'One of the other melachos' — the Chayei Adam, klal 9, writes that this applies specifically where an action was performed upon the object itself whereby it was changed from its original state, as in cooking and similar cases. But one who carries from domain to domain — where the object was not changed — if b'shogeg it is permitted even to him even on that same day, and if b'meizid it is forbidden even to others until Motzei Shabbos immediately. Nevertheless one should be stringent in all Torah-level prohibitions as with cooking. And know that according to the Shulchan Aruch who ruled like R' Yehuda that b'shogeg it is permitted to benefit at Motzei Shabbos — this applies to all melachos where the penalty imposed by the Sages not to benefit on that day until Motzei Shabbos is noticeable. But for one who plants on Shabbos, and the same for one who sows, where in any case he cannot benefit immediately — shogeg equals meizid, and in both cases the planting must be uprooted, as stated explicitly in Gittin 54b in the opinion of R' Yehuda.
54: (1) Introduction to the seif — the Torah forbade performing melacha on Shabbos, and one who performed a melacha on Shabbos b'meizid is liable to death and kares, and b'shogeg is liable to a chatas. The Torah's prohibition is upon the person alone, and not upon the item made on Shabbos in a forbidden manner; however the Sages penalized one who performs a melacha on Shabbos and forbade also the item upon which the melacha was performed, so that people should not treat Shabbos prohibitions lightly. The laws of the penalty are explained in this seif.
56: (2) 'Of the other melachos' — meaning: this seif deals with one who performed any of the melachos forbidden by the Torah on Shabbos, and cooking is only an example. This principle is agreed upon also by the Mechaber.
60: (4) 'After Shabbos' — even if the prohibition was done for their sake. For the Sages did not forbid the item forever, but only upon the one who himself desecrated Shabbos. And the vessels in which he cooked on Shabbos in a forbidden manner are not forbidden.
62: (5) 'Immediately' — and there is no need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu, meaning one does not need to wait after Shabbos until the amount of time it would have taken to perform this melacha had they begun it at the conclusion of Shabbos, as the Rama explains further in the seif.
64: (6) 'Immediately' — meaning: b'shogeg the Sages forbade on that Shabbos itself, so that people should not come to treat Shabbos prohibitions lightly; however they did not distinguish between the shogeg himself and others. All this is in a Torah-level melacha. And in a rabbinic melacha: b'meizid it is forbidden like a Torah-level melacha, however if he acted b'shogeg in a rabbinic melacha — it is permitted to benefit from it even on that Shabbos itself.
66: All this applies to a Torah-level melacha. In a rabbinic melacha: b'meizid it is forbidden like a Torah-level melacha, but if he acted b'shogeg in a rabbinic melacha — it is permitted to benefit from it even on that Shabbos itself.
68: (7) 'Siman 307 seif 20' — there it is explained that regarding the prohibition of instructing a non-Jew the Sages were more stringent, and they forbade benefit from Shabbos labor until Motzei Shabbos b'chedi she'ya'asu. And the reason is that the Sages were more stringent regarding the lighter prohibition of instructing a non-Jew, since they were more concerned that people would come to treat it lightly.
72: (2) One who slaughters on Shabbos for a sick person — whether the person became ill before Shabbos or became ill that day — a healthy person is permitted to eat from it raw {on Shabbos.} But one who cooks {or performed another melacha} for a sick person — it is forbidden {on Shabbos} for a healthy person or for a sick person who is not in danger, for we fear he may increase the quantity for him. {Rama: And even if a non-Jew cooked it, it is forbidden on Shabbos (Tosafos, first chapter of Gittin; Ran, chapter Ein Ma'amidin). And if he cut fruits from something attached to the ground for a sick person on Shabbos, even if the person had been ill from before Shabbos, it is forbidden for a healthy person on Shabbos because it grows and increases on Shabbos and there is the concern of muktzeh (Beit Yosef in the name of the Or Zarua).}
75: (4) 'That he became ill today' — and even though the animal was muktzeh on account of the prohibition of slaughtering, nevertheless it is permitted, for we rule like R' Shimon that there is no muktzeh on account of a prohibition except when he set it aside with his own hands, as in a lamp that was lit on Shabbos [Maggid Mishneh chapter 2]. And it is difficult: if so, muktzeh of something attached should also be permitted when the fruits fell — one can answer that there the reason is lest he climb and detach, as stated at the beginning of Beitza — see there for an additional reason in the Beit Yosef.
77: (5) 'Raw on Shabbos' — and without salting [Tur]; see Yoreh De'ah siman 67 seif 2 that rinsing is nonetheless required, and see siman 325 seif 11.
79: (6) 'Lest he increase for him' — this is a Torah-level prohibition when he increases for him, even before placing the pot on the fire. And there are those who say it is rabbinic — see the Beit Yosef.
81: (7) 'And even if he cooked, etc.' — but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately [Shach], and the reason is that since the non-Jew cooked with permission one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu.
83: (8) 'Because it grows and continues growing' — this refers to fruit whose ripening was not yet complete [Beit Yosef]. But when its ripening has been completed we do not say it grows and increases — for otherwise why would we need in the first chapter of Beitza to forbid something attached because lest he climb and detach, or because of muktzeh? See Tosafos in Bava Kamma 69b that what grows is nullified in the majority; see siman 320 seif 2.
85: (4) 'Raw [meat]' — and without salting [Tur]; see Yoreh De'ah siman 67 seif 2 that rinsing is nonetheless required, and see siman 325 seif 11.
87: (5) 'On Shabbos' — but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately. The Shach explains that since the non-Jew cooked with permission one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu, Magen Avraham. And see Yoreh De'ah siman 113, note 10, where I wrote in the name of the later authorities that it is forbidden even to the sick person himself at Motzei Shabbos — see there.
89: (6) 'And it increases' — this refers to fruit whose ripening is not yet complete [Beit Yosef]. But when its ripening has been completed we do not say it grows and increases — Magen Avraham, see there.
91: (5) 'Or performed another melacha' — for the same reason stated regarding slaughtering, where the permission applies specifically because it is impossible to do otherwise.
93: (6) 'Or for a sick person' — the Rashba writes that this too follows the same reason, for regarding melacha performed by a Jew there is no distinction between him and a healthy person.
95: (7) 'And even' — Tosafos in Gittin explain that what is stated in Eruvin 86 — a non-Jew comforted him alongside his mother — only for circumcision did they permit.
97: (8) 'On Shabbos' — to exclude Motzei Shabbos. And there is no issue of bishul akum since it is not common, there is no concern of intermarriage.
99: (9) 'And if, etc., even, etc.' — this is from Chullin there, such as where one cut a gourd. Meaning, even for a sick person who was ill before Shabbos, similar to the first clause regarding slaughtering — unlike Rashi there. And we do not say that the growths are nullified in the majority of the main fruit, because it is a davar she'yesh lo matirin, as Tosafos wrote in Bava Kamma 69a.
101: (10) 'Because it grows, etc.' — this concern does not apply to an animal, and therefore they were not concerned about this. See Tosafos Yom Tov 37b.
103: (2) 'On Shabbos' — see the Beer Heitev there; and in the matter of the vessels, they are customarily instructed to kasher them by hag'alah three times, as explained in Yoreh De'ah there.
105: (8) 'That he became ill today' — we do not say that the animal is muktzeh because of the prohibition of slaughtering, even though the sick person was not yet ill at twilight and the animal was then muktzeh on account of the prohibition of slaughtering. Nevertheless, since the animal was not set aside by hand but was standing ready for slaughter, it is not muktzeh.
107: (9) 'A healthy person is permitted, etc.' — the reason is that since the primary purpose of the slaughtering is for the sick person, and it is impossible to take even a kezayis of meat without slaughtering, there is no concern that he may increase for him.
109: (10) 'It may be eaten raw on Shabbos' — without salting, since salting is forbidden on Shabbos. And rinsing is required because of visible blood. This is not so for blood that is absorbed within the meat, as long as it has not emerged.
111: (11) 'It is forbidden for the sick person' — but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately, and one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu. And tasting whether the dish is good for the sick person is also permitted on Shabbos.
113: (12) 'Whose life is not in danger' — for he too is like a healthy person regarding this matter, for it is forbidden by Torah law to cook for him through a Jew, and we are concerned that if we permit benefit from this they may increase the amount on Shabbos.
115: (13) 'Lest one increase for him' — to put meat into the pot. This is a Torah-level prohibition when one increases for him, even if he adds everything at once before placing the pot on the fire.
117: (14) 'It is forbidden on Shabbos' — for a healthy person to benefit from it, but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately, and the reason is that since the non-Jew cooked with permission one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu. Also the Sages did not make a decree regarding benefit from a non-Jew's cooking in this unusual case.
119: (15) 'If he was sick before Shabbos' — in that case there may have been intent before Shabbos to detach the fruit for him if needed. However the prohibition of muktzeh still applies since the fruit is attached.
121: (16) 'And there is the concern of muktzeh' — the later authorities asked about these words of the Rama: why is the small amount that grew on Shabbos not nullified in the main fruit? And it appears to explain that we are dealing with vegetables that grow quickly, such as gourds, and the addition that grew on Shabbos is significant. However a fruit like an orange that was detached on Shabbos for a critically ill person, and the sick person ate a slice from it — it is permitted for a healthy person to eat the rest of the fruit.
123: (8) 'One who slaughters on Shabbos for a sick person' — after the previous seif discussed food cooked on Shabbos in violation of the law, this seif discusses food prepared on Shabbos in a permitted manner due to pikuach nefesh, namely for a critically ill person.
125: (9) 'Whether he became ill that day' — one might have thought that if a sick person was already present before Shabbos, we know that tomorrow we will need to slaughter for him; but when he became ill on Shabbos — we did not know this at the entry of Shabbos, and therefore the meat is muktzeh. However as halacha, an animal standing ready for slaughter has its prohibition removed at the moment it is slaughtered, and it is not muktzeh.
127: (10) 'To eat from it raw' — since no prohibition was done here, for it is permitted to slaughter for a critically ill person, and this slaughtering is sufficient for many people without adding any forbidden melachos.
129: (11) 'Another melacha' — the Rama notes that the law is not limited to cooking. It applies to any melacha that resembles cooking and not slaughtering, in that one who performs it for more than one person must increase its performance.
131: (12) 'Lest he increase for him' — lest he intentionally put more into the pot than is needed for the sick person, so that healthy people can also eat from the leftovers.
133: (13) 'It is forbidden on Shabbos' — if a non-Jew cooked for the sick person there is no concern that a Jew will increase, since the non-Jew is permitted to cook, and the prohibition of benefit from a non-Jew's cooking is only rabbinic. Nevertheless the Sages did not make distinctions in their rulings and forbade it even when the non-Jew cooks. But in such a case, at Motzei Shabbos the food is permitted immediately.
135: (14) 'For a sick person on Shabbos' — fruits attached to a tree at the entry of Shabbos are muktzeh machmas issur, since in order to use them on Shabbos he must transgress the prohibition of detaching, and they are forbidden on Shabbos due to muktzeh even if they were detached in a permitted manner, such as by a non-Jew.
137: (15) 'If he was sick before Shabbos' — and then seemingly the fruits are not muktzeh, since his intention was to detach them on Shabbos if the sick person would need them.
139: (16) 'And there is the concern of muktzeh' — the later authorities asked about these words of the Rama: why is the small amount that grew on Shabbos not nullified in the main fruit? And it appears to explain that we are dealing with vegetables that grow quickly, such as gourds, and the addition that grew on Shabbos is significant. However a fruit like an orange that was detached on Shabbos for a critically ill person, and the sick person ate a slice from it — it is permitted for a healthy person to eat the rest of the fruit.
144: (3) Just as it is forbidden to cook with fire, so too it is forbidden to cook with toldos ha'or (derivatives of fire). For example: placing an egg beside a pot, or breaking it on a cloth that was heated by fire, in order to roast it. And even with toldos chamah (derivatives of the sun), such as a cloth heated in the sun — it is forbidden as a decree lest it be confused with toldos ha'or. And likewise it is forbidden to bury it in sand or road dust that was heated by the power of the sun. But in the sun itself — for example placing an egg in the sun, or placing water in the sun to be warmed — it is permitted.
147: (9) 'That it is forbidden to cook' — one who cooks with toldos ha'or is liable.
149: (11) 'Or to break it, etc., and even, etc., but' — three distinctions regarding the egg in Beitza 2b, see Rashi there.
151: (3) 'To insulate it' — see the Beer Heitev. See also Noda B'Yehuda second edition, chapter 23, who writes that the rule that salted is like heated applies specifically to roasting, and is a Torah-level matter regarding absorption like a vessel; but it cannot be considered like roasting to render it forbidden as bishul on Shabbos or to forbid Pesach meat that was salted on account of roasting — see there.
153: (17) 'With toldos ha'or' — one who cooks with them is liable. Therefore, one who places fruits or water on the oven or inside the heating stove after the oven has been fired up, and they cooked there, is liable. And by rabbinic law it is forbidden to place them even before the oven is fired up, as explained later. And all the laws of cooking mentioned in this siman apply also to something cooked by means of toldos ha'or.
155: (18) 'And even with derivatives of the sun' — even b'dieved it is forbidden, and it is possible that after Shabbos it is permitted even to the one who cooked [Chiddushei R' Akiva Eiger].
157: (19) 'To insulate it, etc.' — this applies even before Shabbos, because sand is something that adds heat, as explained above in siman 257 seif 3, and it is forbidden to insulate with it even before Shabbos as explained there.
159: (20) 'In sand' — even if one does not insulate it but merely rolls it on Shabbos on hot sand so that it will roast, it is also forbidden as a decree on account of toldos ha'or. Therefore it is forbidden to roast an egg on Shabbos in sand heated by the sun.
161: (21) 'But in the sun itself' — the Sages did not decree on account of fire, for the sun and fire are not confused with each other.
164: 'And even in derivatives of the sun, etc.' — see the Mishna Berurah that leaving food in derivatives of the sun is permitted, and in Chiddushei R' Akiva Eiger he inclines to say that even in toldos ha'or it is permitted to leave food, for it is no worse than a swept-out stove — see there. And to insulate in sand heated by the sun is forbidden according to all.
166: 'To insulate it in sand' — see the Peri Megadim who writes that even if the egg is fully roasted it is still forbidden to insulate it, for the prohibition of insulating applies even to something fully cooked as written in siman 257. And one should also examine the Gra there.
169: (17) Introduction to the seif — there is no Torah prohibition of cooking except through heat from fire. The prohibition includes both cooking directly with fire, such as roasting or cooking on a stove, and cooking with something that was heated by fire (toldos ha'or). The Sages decreed that cooking with toldos chamah (derivatives of the sun) is also forbidden as a decree lest it be confused with toldos ha'or.
171: (18) 'With fire' — with heat from fire, and its prohibition is by Torah law.
173: (19) 'With toldos ha'or' — with something that was heated by fire, and this is also a Torah-level prohibition.
175: (20) 'So that it will roast' — these are examples of cooking on something that has been heated by fire, which is not cooking directly on the fire.
177: (21) 'With derivatives of the sun' — with something that was heated by the force of the sun, and it is also forbidden to cook with it.
179: (22) 'As a decree on account of toldos ha'or' — because a cloth heated by the sun resembles a cloth heated by fire, which is forbidden to cook with by Torah law, and therefore the Sages decreed against it.
181: (23) 'From the power of the sun' — and the prohibition is by rabbinic law.
183: (24) 'It is permitted' — because there is no concern that people will confuse heating directly in the sun with heating by fire.
185: The law of a solar water heater is like water boiled in the sun, which is permitted to use on Shabbos. And a solar heater combined with an electric heater is permitted only if the electricity was not activated on erev Shabbos.
189: (4) A dish that was fully cooked: there is a concern of cooking if it cooled. {Rama: And some say that this applies only when it is mitzamek v'yafeh lo — continued cooking improves it — but when it is mitzamek v'ra lo — continued cooking harms it — it is permitted. And this is the primary ruling. But one who cooks something that is not fully cooked — even while it is still boiling — violates a Torah prohibition. These words apply to a dish with broth; but a dry item that was fully cooked, even if it cooled, it is permitted to soak it in hot water. But one rinses it with hot water on Shabbos. Except for old salted fish and kolyas ha'ispanin, for their rinsing completes their cooking and they are liable; and the same applies to any hard item.}
192: (4) 'Some say the restriction applies only in certain cases, etc.' — but when further cooking would harm the food (mitzamek v'ra lo), it is permitted. So wrote the Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu Yeruham, who wrote that when something cooled and is mitzamek v'yafeh lo one should not place it so close to a fire where the hand is scalded. But if it is mitzamek v'ra lo it is permitted to place it there.
194: (5) 'Except for old salted fish, etc.' — this implies that with cold water it is permitted, and therefore it is permitted to rinse herring on Shabbos with cold water even if it is very salty, and so wrote the Beit Yosef at the end of this siman in the name of the Poskim.
196: (11) 'There is a concern of cooking' — know that whenever something is forbidden because of cooking, it is forbidden even to place it on the stove or oven before the fire is lit, as written at the end of siman 253.
198: (12) 'If it cooled' — the Beit Yosef infers that as long as the food is still yad soledes bo it is still considered at full boil. And so writes Rabbeinu Yeruham: if it has not cooled, even if it changed somewhat from its boiling, it is permitted — see seif 15 in the Rama's gloss.
200: (13) 'Some say, specifically, etc.' — the Bach ruled like the first view. See what the Mishna Berurah wrote.
202: (14) 'One may soak it — even in a kli rishon — for there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking, as stated in seif 15; and so wrote Tosafos, the Mordechai, and the Ran — not like the Bach who is stringent. And it is implied from the language of the Shulchan Aruch that if it was not cooked before Shabbos but was only soaked in hot water, it is forbidden to soak it in hot water on Shabbos.
204: (15) 'One rinses it' — meaning, one pours onto it from a kli sheni [and some are lenient even for a wet item]. But soaking is forbidden even in a kli sheni, for it appears like cooking — it is not comparable to spices in seif 9.
206: (16) 'Any hard item' — the same applies to something salty that cannot be eaten at all without rinsing (Beit Yosef). The Gemara states that if he rinsed it he is liable.
208: (8) 'Cooking' — know that whenever something is forbidden because of cooking, it is forbidden even to place it on the stove or oven before the fire is lit, as written at the end of siman 253. Magen Avraham.
210: (9) 'Some say' — the Bach ruled like the first view; see what the Mishna Berurah wrote.
212: (10) 'To soak it — even in a kli rishon — as in seif 15, for there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking. It is implied from the language of the Shulchan Aruch that if it was not cooked before Shabbos but was only soaked in hot water, it is forbidden to soak it in hot water on Shabbos.
214: (11) 'One rinses it' — meaning, one pours onto it from a kli sheni; soaking is forbidden even in a kli sheni because it appears like cooking. It is not comparable to spices in seif 9.
216: (12) 'Old salted fish' — this implies that with cold water it is permitted; therefore it is permitted to rinse herring on Shabbos with cold water even if it is very salty.
218: (13) 'A hard item' — the same applies to something salty that cannot be eaten at all without rinsing (Beit Yosef). The Gemara states that if he rinsed it he is liable.
220: (12) 'A cooked dish' — not like the concern 'lest he stir it' as Rashi explains, and even if it was fully cooked, as Tosafos wrote in Shabbos 47b s.v. b'mah. In ordinary pots, etc.
222: (13) 'Some say' — this fits what is written at the end of seif 8 in the name of Rabbeinu Yeruham. But from what is written in siman 257 seif 7, it is implied that it is forbidden according to all. And Rabbeinu Yeruham possibly does not hold this ruling.
224: (14) 'And if not [fully cooked]' — from what is said in the fourth chapter of Yom Tov regarding the concern lest one stir it, meaning lest one stir the pot and hasten the cooking.
226: (16) 'The same applies' — we learn from the above that their rinsing completes their melacha; see chapter Kira: 'rolling — what about it? — so too we' — which implies that the same applies to anything that constitutes completion of the melacha.
228: (22) 'There is a concern of cooking' — all rulings forbidden because of cooking apply even to placing food on the stove or in the oven before the fire is lit, as written in siman 253.
230: (23) 'Cooking' — therefore it is forbidden by Torah law to leave this dish on Shabbos in a place where the hand is scalded in it. And to mix it into a boiling dish in a kli sheni there are grounds for leniency [later authorities].
232: (24) 'If it cooled' — meaning that it is no longer yad soledes bo, even though it is still somewhat warm. But if it is still yad soledes bo even though it changed somewhat from its full boil, cooking no longer applies to it.
234: (25) 'Mitzamek v'yafeh lo' — continued cooking improves it — but if it is mitzamek v'ra lo it is permitted to place it close to a fire even in a place where the hand is scalded; see the Bach who ruled like the first view that there is no distinction in this.
236: (26) 'The same applies further' — until its cooking is finished, the prohibition of cooking by Torah law still applies.
238: (27) 'Even while still boiling' — it is obvious that even indirectly one may not complete the cooking. It appears that b'dieved one should not forbid the dish, for there are authorities who hold that cooking after cooking in broth where the dish cooled is only rabbinic.
240: (28) 'These words' — meaning what we said — that once it cooled, cooking applies in every form — refers to a dish that has broth.
242: (29) 'Broth' — for a wet item, once its heat dissipates and it cools, the status of its first cooking no longer applies.
244: (30) 'But a dry item' — when it was fully cooked.
246: (31) 'Already cooked' — means actually cooked; but if it was not cooked and was only soaked on erev Shabbos in a kli rishon that is yad soledes bo, it is forbidden to soak it in hot water that is yad soledes bo on Shabbos, even though there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking — since the item was not actually cooked, this exemption does not apply.
248: (32) 'And it is dry' — meaning they poured the sauce off it.
250: (33) 'One may soak it — even in a boiling kli rishon — until it softens and becomes wet, for there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking. But one may not place it in a kli rishon standing on the fire.
252: (34) '[Soaking] it in hot water that is yad soledes bo — even without leaving food there until it softens — and even in a kli sheni it is forbidden to soak, for it appears like cooking. It is not comparable to spices, for spices are made to flavor the pot.
254: (35) 'One rinses it' — meaning one pours onto it from a kli sheni. From a kli rishon it is forbidden to pour onto it, for pouring from a kli rishon is like a kli rishon and cooks the outer layer, as written in seif 10.
256: (36) 'Except for old salted fish' — salted fish from the previous year, and kolyas ha'ispanin is the name of a fish that is eaten by rinsing it in hot water on account of its saltiness. Therefore even pouring from a kli rishon on them constitutes cooking for them, since they need heat to become edible.
258: (37) 'Their rinsing, etc.' — in hot water as above; in cold water one may rinse and even soak, even for something that becomes fit to eat through soaking in cold water, since any item that is not fit to eat raw is not subject to the prohibition of cooking.
260: (38) 'The same applies to any hard item' — meaning something fit to eat raw without cooking, but so dry and hard that it cannot be eaten at all on account of this without soaking in hot water.
262: (39) 'That it is forbidden to soak' — even in a kli sheni. The same is true if something would become fit to eat through mere rinsing in hot water — even rinsing is forbidden, as above regarding old salted fish.
264: (25) 'Fully cooked' — an ordinary cooked dish usually contains broth, as explained below.
266: (26) 'If it cooled' — even though this dish was already cooked, the leniency 'there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking' applies only to a dry item. But a liquid that cooled, when it is reheated, is re-cooked.
268: (27) 'Mitzamek v'yafeh lo' — continued cooking improves it — according to this view the prohibition of cooking in a wet dish that cooled applies only when it is mitzamek v'yafeh lo, but if it is mitzamek v'ra lo there is no prohibition of cooking and it is permitted to reheat it.
270: (28) 'Maachal ben Drusai' — this is the name given to food that is barely edible. Its measure is that it has cooked half the time needed for full cooking. The name derives from a bandit named ben Drusai who ate his food barely cooked.
272: (29) 'While it is still boiling' — as long as the cooking is not complete, the cooking process continues, and one violates a Torah-level prohibition of cooking.
274: (30) 'To soak it in hot water on Shabbos' — since there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking for a dry item, because the heat does not materially change the food. Unlike a liquid, which changes materially upon reheating.
276: (31) 'In hot water on Shabbos' — meaning, one may not place it into hot water in a kli rishon, even if the kli has been removed from the fire. This is forbidden by Torah law for items that cook in a kli rishon.
278: (32) 'One may rinse it with hot water on Shabbos' — meaning, according to this view, one may pour hot water over it from a kli rishon, because pouring from a kli rishon does not cook. But the Mechaber's words in seif 10 that forbid pouring from a kli rishon on spices refer to spices which are not fully cooked.
280: (33) 'Old salted fish' — fish that was salted for preservation, and it is impossible to eat it as-is because of its saltiness.
282: (34) 'Their completion is achieved' — their completion is achieved by rinsing them from a kli rishon, and one is liable for them on account of cooking even through pouring from a kli rishon. The general rule is that a kli sheni does not cook, except for items that require heat to become edible.
284: (35) 'A hard item' — meaning an item that is not cooked.
286: (36) 'Completion of the melacha' — it is forbidden because this completes the cooking process. It appears as halacha that if a food can visibly be seen to cook in a kli sheni and becomes edible through it — even in a kli sheni one is liable.
289: (3) 'A cooked dish that was fully cooked, etc.' — this is the opinion of Rashi who explains regarding what is stated in the first chapter of Shabbos that one may place wool in a cauldron close to Shabbos — and we should be concerned lest he stir it — he explained: lest he stir the pot itself to make the wool take the dye better.
292: 'If it cooled' — see the Mishna Berurah: this means it is no longer yad soledes bo. If it was poured into another vessel, even if it was still yad soledes bo there are grounds to say it has the status of having cooled.
294: 'It is their completion' — at first glance it appears that this too applies specifically when the water is yad soledes bo, similar to the rinsing case at the beginning of the seif where certainly it is permitted even in hot water that is yad soledes bo. But if we examine the matter it appears that even in water that is not yad soledes bo it is forbidden.
296: 'The same applies to any hard item' — see the Mishna Berurah who asks why it was necessary to conclude that this is the completion of its melacha — see there. Alternatively one can say that the Hagas Mordechai holds like the Mordechai who explained in siman 257 that a kli sheni does not cook at all.
298: 'Because this is the completion of its melacha' — see the Mishna Berurah regarding brewing tea. See what we wrote there, that one should place the cold essence into the cup from which he drinks after pouring the hot water — and thus there is no prohibition.
300: This permission is by Torah law. But we have already seen in siman 253 seif 2 that the Sages forbade placing even cooked food on a heat source intended for cooking, lest it appear as if he is cooking.
302: The definition of dry food for this matter is any solid food that is not submerged in broth or oil. Even if it has a small amount of sauce on it, it is permitted to heat it.
304: There are poskim — including the Magen Avraham and Mishna Berurah note 35 — who forbid any soaking in a kli sheni, because it appears like cooking, and they explain the Mechaber's words as referring to rinsing only, not soaking.
309: (5) Some say that something baked or roasted, if one then cooks it in broth, there is a concern of cooking, and it is forbidden to place bread even in a kli sheni that is yad soledes bo. And some permit. {Rama: In a kli sheni. And some are lenient even in a kli rishon. And the custom is to be careful l'chatchila not to place bread even in a kli sheni as long as the hand is scalded in it.}
312: (6) 'If one cooked it afterward, etc.' — the Tur wrote this in the name of R' Eliezer Metz: even though there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking for a dry item, nevertheless there is cooking after roasting. His proof is from the chapter of kol sha'ah regarding a Passover offering — if one roasted it and then cooked it, one is liable. The Ravyah disagreed, and the Beit Yosef praised the Ravyah's challenge as strong.
314: (7) 'Even in a kli sheni' — the reason given in the Beit Yosef is that bread may easily cook even in a kli sheni. And those who permit hold like the Tur, that we do not find cooking in a kli sheni except for salt according to one opinion. See seif 9.
316: (8) 'And the custom is to be careful l'chatchila' — meaning that they do not place bread in the cholent broth, and it appears to me that those who slice onions very thin and place them in the broth should not place them while the hand is still scalded. And from what is written further in the gloss, the custom emerged to be careful even in a kli sheni, and b'dieved one should not forbid even in a kli rishon.
318: (17) 'Because of cooking' — even though there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking, there is cooking after roasting. And likewise there is roasting after cooking. Therefore it is forbidden to place something cooked near the fire without any vessel, for the heat would roast it.
320: (18) 'Even in a kli sheni' — for there are items that cook in it and we are not expert in all of them, and therefore for other items as well one should be stringent — see seif 9.
322: (19) 'Those who permit' — according to the view that a kli sheni does not cook, and from what was written in seif 4 in the name of Tosafos one should be stringent for it appears like cooking; but those who permit hold that according to the second answer in seif 9 there is no concern here.
324: (20) 'Even in a kli rishon' — since it is dry there is no cooking after baking.
326: (14) 'Cooking' — even though there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking for a fully cooked item, there is cooking after roasting. And likewise there is roasting after cooking.
328: (15) 'Even in a kli sheni' — the reason given in the Beit Yosef is that perhaps bread, because it softens easily, is cooked even in a kli sheni. And those who permit hold like the Tur, that we do not find cooking in a kli sheni except for salt according to one opinion.
330: (16) 'In a kli rishon' — since it is dry there is no cooking after baking.
332: (17) 'As long as the hand is scalded in it' — meaning that bread should not be put in the broth as long as the hand is scalded, and it appears to me that those who slice onions very thin and place them in the broth should not place them until after taking the pot off the fire.
334: (17) 'There is one who says' — like R' Yosi, Pesachim 41a, and likewise regarding Pesach where one roasted it, etc.
336: (18) 'Even in a kli sheni' — Shabbos 42b, and even according to the second version, because salt requires cooking, etc. But other items agree with the first version.
338: (19) 'And there is' — as written there 40b and the Magen Avraham, and according to the second version the first version is rejected.
340: (20) 'And some explain' — see Tosafos in Pesachim there s.v. Ula, etc. And we rule in Berachos there that boiled vegetables receive the blessing borei pri ha'adamah, and in Pesachim it is written that Ula holds that for blessings we require the taste of matza.
342: (4) 'Cooking' — see the Beer Heitev and see Noda B'Yehuda responsum: if there is nothing but water alone in a kli sheni, it is forbidden to place ground coffee into it since it changes its appearance.
344: (40) 'If it is cooked later in a liquid' — meaning that we placed it in a pot when it is being cooked with sauce. If we placed it in cold liquids, the problem would be cooking the liquids themselves.
346: (41) 'Because of cooking' — even though there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking for a dry item, there is cooking after roasting, even while still hot from the roasting [later authorities]. And likewise there is roasting after cooking.
348: (42) 'And it is forbidden to place bread, etc.' — he added another law here, and the reason for this opinion is that he holds there are items that cook even in a kli sheni because they are soft.
350: (43) 'Those who permit in a kli sheni' — he holds that a kli sheni does not cook anything.
352: (44) 'Even in a kli rishon' — he holds that the concept of cooking after baking or roasting does not apply, and the same in reverse.
354: (45) 'And the custom is to be careful, etc.' — meaning that they would not put bread into the cholent broth in the bowl which is a kli sheni, and all the more so one should be careful not to pour onto it from a kli rishon.
356: (46) 'L'chatchila, etc.' — and b'dieved even in a kli rishon one should not forbid, for there are those who are lenient.
358: (47) 'Even in a kli sheni' — regarding a kli shelishi, the Peri Megadim in the Eshel Avraham inclines toward leniency — see there.
360: (48) 'As long as the hand is scalded in it' — see the Chayei Adam who writes that where the hand is burned, all agree it cooks even in a kli sheni.
362: (37) 'Because of cooking' — we saw above the rule that there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking. The poskim disagree whether this rule applies only to cooking after cooking, or also to cooking after baking and roasting.
364: (38) 'When it is yad soledes bo' — according to the view that forbids cooking after baking, bread involves cooking. The Mechaber states that this is forbidden even in a kli sheni.
366: (39) 'And some permit — even in a kli rishon — for they are not concerned about cooking after baking. The Mechaber's view is that in this matter one may be lenient even in a kli rishon that is not on the fire.
368: (40) 'In a kli sheni' — according to this view there is cooking after baking and roasting; but specifically in a kli rishon, since a kli sheni does not cook even what has not previously been cooked.
370: (41) 'Even in a kli rishon — to place bread' — according to that view there is no cooking even after baking and roasting, and cooking bread is not rendering it fit to eat but only softening it.
372: (42) 'When it is yad soledes bo' — to take into account the view that although a kli sheni does not cook what is not cooked at all, it does cook what was baked or roasted.
375: 'Some say, etc., because of cooking' — see the Mishna Berurah — that there is also roasting after cooking; and see the Peri Megadim who cites Pesachim 41 that the first cooking was not annulled.
377: Summary of cooking after baking: the Shulchan Aruch is lenient in this matter, and the Rama agrees in principle, but the custom is to be stringent even in a kli sheni. And b'dieved if one placed bread even in a kli rishon that is not on the fire, one should not forbid it.
382: (6) A vessel containing something hot that is yad soledes bo — it is permitted to place it on Shabbos on top of a pot that is buried in garments, even in a place where the upper one can become warm. And he may seal its mouth with dough. But one may not place a cold dish on it in a place where the upper one could become yad soledes bo.
385: (9) 'A hot thing that is yad soledes bo' — and even if it was not fully cooked, for we said above that even when it is boiling there is still a concern of cooking. This case is different because it cannot come to full cooking, for the pot insulates it.
387: (10) 'To seal its mouth with dough' — it is difficult, for smearing means spreading, and in the Aruch it is written that plastering, smearing, and spreading are all one. If so, what is the difference from the case in chapter Chavis brought in siman 314 seif 11?
389: (11) 'That is yad soledes bo' — see what was written in seif 4 and seif 15 in the gloss.
391: (22) 'In dough' — but with something that spreads it is forbidden as written in siman 314 seif 11.
393: (23) 'One may not place, etc.' — and for a dry item it is permitted — see seif 8.
395: (18) 'Scalded' — even if it was not fully cooked, it is permitted since here only the heat is being preserved and it cannot come to full cooking — Taz, see there; and see seif 15.
397: (19) 'In dough' — but for something that spreads it is forbidden as written in siman 314 seif 11; and see the Taz.
399: (20) 'Hot' — and for a dry item it is permitted — see seif 8.
403: (22) 'But' — there, and not that it would be heated, and as Tosafos wrote Shabbos 48a s.v. what is different, etc.
405: (49) 'A hot thing where the hand is scalded, etc.' — the Mechaber follows his view in seif 4 that if it cooled somewhat until the hand is no longer scalded in it, there is again a concern of cooking. But according to what is written in seif 15 in the gloss, the custom is to be lenient as long as it has not completely cooled.
407: (50) 'In it' — and even if it was not fully cooked, for we said above in seif 4 that there is a concern of cooking even when it is boiling. This case is different because it cannot come to full cooking through this, since the pot below insulates it.
409: (51) 'To place it, etc., in the buried pot' — in garments from before Shabbos. And it teaches us that it is permitted to place the vessel under the garments covering the pot, even though one may not insulate on Shabbos even without adding heat, because here the main insulating was done for the pot and this vessel is only secondary.
411: (52) 'Sealing its mouth with dough' — so that its heat does not escape. And we are dealing with dough that is not muktzeh, such as that needed for the chickens in his house. And see the Magen Avraham that specifically dough that is not susceptible to baking is meant.
413: (53) 'But one may not place, etc.' — a dish that cooled — we rule in seif 4 that there is cooking after cooking, and therefore it is forbidden even without any insulating at all. And this applies to a wet item. But for a dry item it is permitted — see seif 8.
415: (54) 'That the upper one can become warm, etc.' — meaning even if he does not intend to leave it there that long, we are concerned lest he forget, as is stated later in seif 14.
417: (43) 'And it will not cool' — we saw in siman 257 that insulating (covering a hot pot on all sides) on erev Shabbos is forbidden with something that adds heat, and on Shabbos itself it is forbidden in any case. And here it is permitted since the main purpose is to keep the lower pot warm.
419: (44) 'To seal its mouth with dough' — unrelated to insulating. A hot vessel that wishes to preserve its heat on Shabbos, it is permitted to seal its opening with dough, and there is no prohibition of cooking or insulating in this. And here we are speaking of placing dough, not spreading it, which is forbidden on Shabbos.
421: (45) 'That was kneaded yesterday' — because kneading dough on Shabbos is forbidden by Torah law.
423: (46) 'It is yad soledes bo' — this refers to a broth dish where there is cooking after cooking if the hand is no longer scalded from its heat. And in seif 15 the Rama will be lenient regarding a wet dish whose heat dropped below yad soledes bo, as long as it has not completely cooled.
426: 'And he may seal its mouth with dough' — this implies that dough is permitted to be placed on a hot vessel where the hand is scalded, and we are not concerned that it will come to partial baking to form a crust [see above in siman 254 seif 5 regarding the measure for bread].
428: 'Until it becomes yad soledes bo' — but if it cannot reach that level of heat, it is permitted to place it there even when completely cold, even though it will warm up somewhat.
433: (7) Some explain that it is permitted to place a vessel containing a hot item on top of a buried pot, even if the lower vessel is on the fire. And some explain that if the lower vessel is on the fire, it is forever forbidden.
436: (11) 'Even if the lower vessel is on the fire' — the Maggid Mishneh wrote the reason: since the pot interrupts, this is like warming against a fire and it is permitted. It appears that this also applies specifically in a place where it cannot come to full cooking.
438: (24) 'It is never forbidden' — this is comparable to placing on a stove l'chatchila on Shabbos (Rabbeinu Yeruham). And therefore, based on what is written in siman 253 seif 2, if one removed it from on top of the stove after nightfall, it is permitted to place it on a pot — see there.
440: (11) 'Forbidden' — for it is comparable to placing on a stove l'chatchila on Shabbos — Rabbeinu Yeruham. And therefore based on what is written in siman 253 seif 2, if one removed it from on top of the stove after nightfall, it is permitted to place it on a pot — see there.
442: (23) 'Oil and water' — the rule is that anything for which cooking is permitted opposite the fire is also permitted with toldos ha'or, as stated in Shabbos 40b: 'according to the one who says oil has no concern of cooking, it is permitted opposite the fire.'
444: (55) 'Even the lower vessel, etc.' — the reason is that since the pot interrupts, there is a recognizable distinction and it does not appear as if he is cooking. And we are speaking of a vessel that was fully cooked.
446: (56) 'On the fire, etc.' — he holds that a pot that interrupts is like a swept-out stove, which it is forbidden to place food on l'chatchila, and see what we wrote below that the halacha follows the first view.
448: (47) 'The buried pot' — this is the permission we saw at the beginning of the previous seif.
450: (48) 'Permitted' — according to this view there is no prohibition of cooking, since we are dealing with a hot cooked dish and there is no cooking after cooking. There is also no concern of appearing to cook.
452: (49) 'It is never forbidden' — according to this method, since the lower pot is on the fire, placing on it is like placing on a stove on Shabbos, which is forbidden even if the stove is swept out.
457: (8) To place a cold item that was fully cooked on top of a meicham that is on the fire: some say its law is like placing on a stove, and it is forbidden even for something that has no concern of cooking. And some say that the first view appears to be the primary one; and anything that is permitted to place there according to seif 4 is permitted here, as long as it is not mitzamek v'yafeh lo.
460: (25) 'Like placing on a stove' — even for something that has no concern of cooking it is forbidden to place it on the stove, since we decree lest he rake the coals.
462: (26) 'And the first view appears to be the primary one' — since the pot interrupts, it is not comparable to the stove, where the pot stands directly on the fire [Maggid Mishneh chapter 22]. This requires investigation as to why the Beit Yosef did not decide in seif 7.
464: (27) 'And mitzamek v'yafeh lo' — this is the language of Rabbeinu Yeruham, and it is the Rama's gloss in seif 4. And this requires investigation since the Beit Yosef in seif 4 ruled not like him.
466: (22) 'Stove' — even for something that has no concern of cooking it is forbidden to place it on the stove, since we decree lest he rake the coals.
468: (23) 'The primary thing' — since the pot interrupts, unlike the stove where the pot stands directly on the fire. Maggid Mishneh chapter 22. And see the Magen Avraham.
470: (24) 'Seif 8, and anything that is permitted, etc.' — same as what is learned from oil.
472: (25) 'Even if' — as written in siman 253: if it was not fully cooked the return is forbidden as written there seif 2. And mitzamek v'ra lo is learned from hot water as written there. And the same applies to preserving heat as written there seif 3.
474: (26) 'And mitzamek' — according to his method as written in seif 4 in the gloss, and see the Magen Avraham.
476: (57) 'To place a cold item' — seif 8 and seif 7 are one matter, and these two opinions in seif 8 are the same as those in seif 7, except that seif 7 deals with a wet item and seif 8 with a dry item.
478: (58) 'And anything that is permitted to place, etc.' — meaning everything described in seif 4 as having no concern of cooking, such as a dry item even if it cooled, and it is permitted to soak it in a kli rishon; but for a wet item that cooled, it is forbidden since there is cooking after cooking.
480: (59) 'Meicham on the fire' — and even though even on a swept-out stove it is not permitted in siman 253 except to return food, to place l'chatchila is forbidden as stated there in seif 5. This is the meicham with its full contents, and the pot interrupts.
482: (60) 'The first view appears to be the primary position' — and so ruled the Eliyah Rabbah and the Biur HaGra. And this also applies to the matter of seif 7, for they are one matter as we wrote above.
484: (61) 'Sauce' — a dish that has sauce — the Mechaber already ruled above in seif 4 that when it cooled there is cooking after cooking. Therefore it is forbidden to place it on a hot meicham even if it is not on the fire.
486: (62) 'And mitzamek v'yafeh lo' — know that the entire language of this seif is from the language of Rabbeinu Yeruham following his approach mentioned above in seif 4 in the gloss, that specifically when it is mitzamek v'yafeh lo is there cooking after cooking for a broth dish that cooled.
489: 'Some say that it is comparable to placing on a stove' — and according to this opinion even if it is dry and was hot it is also forbidden.
491: 'And mitzamek, etc., is forbidden according to all' — meaning even according to the first view, and all this is according to the Rosh and the Shulchan Aruch seif 4. But according to the Maggid Mishneh quoted in seif 15 in the gloss, that even something that has broth and is lukewarm and not mitzamek, there is no cooking after cooking — then mitzamek v'yafeh lo is the primary stringency.
494: (50) Introduction to the seif — this seif, like the previous one, deals with placing food on top of a pot that is on the fire; but the previous seif deals with placing on top of a buried pot, and this seif deals with placing on top of a meicham full of water.
496: (51) 'Fully cooked' — and therefore there is no Torah prohibition of cooking.
498: (52) 'Like placing opposite the fire' — in seifs 14-15 below it will be explained that it is permitted to place a dry item opposite the fire, while it is forbidden to place a wet item in a place where it can reach yad soledes bo.
500: (53) 'Such as it is dry' — and then there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking.
502: (54) 'On the fire' — there is no concern here of appearing to cook, because there is no way to cook on top of a full pot.
504: (55) 'To preserve its heat' — the opinion of those who say it is forbidden: even though the lower pot is full of water and not empty, the one who places a pot on top of it appears to be cooking.
506: (56) 'And the first view appears to be the primary one' — to permit placing on Shabbos on top of a meicham that is on the fire. And in a rabbinic doubt we follow the lenient view.
508: (57) 'That has sauce in it' — and it cooled.
510: (58) 'And mitzamek v'yafeh lo' — meaning that the cooked dish with the sauce cooled, and moreover the continued cooking improves it.
512: (59) 'According to all' — because of the Torah prohibition of cooking.
516: (9) A kli rishon — meaning the vessel that was used on the fire — cooks even after it has been removed from the fire, as long as the hand is scalded in it. Therefore it is forbidden to place spices in it, or even salted meat; but bull's meat [meaning meat that is hard to cook] is permitted. And salted meat — because of the blood in it — is forbidden. And one who puts salt in a kli rishon — even though it was removed from the fire — a blessing comes upon him if he did not violate a prohibition. {Rama: And the more stringent one is praiseworthy. And one who places salted meat in it when it is on the fire — even if not salted — is also forbidden.}
519: (12) 'Even after it has been removed, etc.' — the Beit Yosef wrote in the name of the Hagahot Mordechai that it is closest to say that it is only called a kli rishon from the moment it is removed from the fire, but if one left it to cool even in a place where the hand is scalded in it, it loses its status as a kli rishon.
521: (13) 'Salted meat' — the Rosh wrote that it implies bull's meat is not cooked in a kli rishon and it is permitted to place raw meat in a kli rishon that was removed from the fire. However if it is old salt it causes cooking.
523: (14) 'And some forbid placing salt' — in the Gemara there are two versions. According to the second version, salt is treated leniently since it is hard to cook like bull's meat — therefore it is permitted even in a kli rishon. According to the first version it is treated stringently since it requires cooking — therefore it is forbidden even in a kli sheni.
525: (15) 'Nullified on top of the food' — and it is not a davar she'yesh lo matirin after Shabbos, since even in a thousand it would not be nullified. But here it is nullified before the prohibition takes effect, since salt does not cook except in a kli rishon, and it is nullified before it cooks.
527: (28) 'As long as it is yad soledes bo' — and it appears to me that if it is not yad soledes bo it is permitted, even though for the matter of forbidden and permitted there are those who forbid, as written in Toras Chatas klal 57 — that is because it absorbs and expels.
529: (29) 'Of bull' — the fact that the meat does not cook — the moisture within it cooks (Tur).
531: (30) 'Blood in it' — and we are dealing with meat that was rinsed after salting, otherwise it is still forbidden because of the blood in it. And the clear intent of the Beit Yosef implies specifically when it is still salted does placing it in a kli rishon render the blood forbidden.
533: (31) 'The salt is nullified in sixty' — and even though something that imparts flavor is not nullified — here it is different for it is zeh v'zeh gorem, since it was already salted before Shabbos as well. And even though a davar she'yesh lo matirin is not nullified, since this applies after Shabbos it is nullified before the prohibition.
535: (24) 'Scalded' — see the Magen Avraham and see Yoreh De'ah siman 94 note 2 what is written there in the name of the Maharshal.
537: (25) 'Of bull' — the fact that the meat does not cook — the moisture within it cooks. Tur.
539: (26) 'Blood' — and we are dealing with meat that was rinsed after salting, otherwise it is still forbidden because of the blood in the salt. And the clear intent of the Beit Yosef implies specifically when it is still salted the blood becomes forbidden.
541: (27) 'Salt' — I have already written in note 17 that the same applies to onions since they are sharp and cook quickly, and we observe that when placed in a hot kli sheni they become visibly soft.
543: (28) 'Nullified' — see the Taz who disagrees and concluded that this eating should not be permitted on Shabbos but one should wait until after Shabbos — see there, and see the Magen Avraham.
545: (27) 'Seif 9 is forbidden according to all' — meaning even according to the first view, and all this is according to the Rosh and Shulchan Aruch seif 4. But according to the Maggid Mishneh cited in seif 15 in the gloss.
547: (28) 'As long as the hand is scalded in it' — if it is not yad soledes bo, there is no concern of cooking. This is why throughout this siman it states 'the hand is scalded,' and even a kli rishon that is not yad soledes bo is considered like a kli sheni.
549: (29) 'Since they removed it' — Rashi there s.v. dib'chli.
551: (30) 'And there is' — the Rosh there, and see the Taz in the name of the Rosh; the Tur did not mention salted meat.
553: (31) 'And some forbid' — like the first version.
555: (32) 'And those who are stringent' — Tosafos there.
557: (33) 'Even he, etc.' — on the fire even according to the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch it is forbidden as stated above.
559: (34) 'The salt' — see the Magen Avraham. And what is written regarding something that imparts flavor — see in Chullin 97b and in Avodah Zarah 69a. And what is written regarding zeh v'zeh gorem — see in Pesachim 26-27.
561: (5) 'Nullified' — see the Beer Heitev and the Peri Megadim, siman 84: those who bring hot water in a kli rishon on Shabbos that is fully boiled — if one erred and poured from the kli rishon into small bowls that have ground spices in them, if the bowls are kli sheni the spices are not forbidden.
563: (59) 'All the time, etc.' — meaning even after it has stopped boiling.
565: (60) 'The hand is scalded in it' — but if the hand is not scalded in it, even a kli rishon does not cook. And if it was not removed from the fire it is forbidden to place spices in it.
567: (61) 'To place spices in it' — but in a kli sheni it is permitted to place spices even when yad soledes bo, since they do not cook there. And if a solid item is placed in a kli sheni that is yad soledes bo there are grounds for stringency.
569: (62) 'Since they removed it' — on the fire, even bull's meat cooks.
571: (63) 'Like bull's meat' — and even though it melts even in a kli sheni, its melting is not its cooking, for even in cold you see the same thing.
573: (64) 'Salted meat' — meaning meat that was salted and rinsed according to the law.
575: (65) 'Of bull' — the fact that the meat does not cook — the moisture within it cooks [Tur].
577: (66) 'Without salting, etc.' — we were not led to think that the reason it is forbidden is because the salt softens the meat and it then cooks in a kli rishon. Rather even without being salted the moisture within it cooks.
579: (67) 'And some forbid, etc.' — in the Gemara there are two versions: according to the second version, salt is treated leniently since it is hard to cook like bull's meat — therefore it is permitted even in a kli rishon. According to the first version it needs cooking — therefore it is forbidden even in a kli sheni.
581: (68) 'Even he, etc.' — on the fire even according to the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch it is forbidden, as above.
583: (69) 'The salt is nullified' — even though something that imparts flavor is not nullified, here it is different for it is zeh v'zeh gorem — here we are dealing with meat that was already salted before Shabbos as well, and the salt was already absorbed into the meat.
585: (60) 'The hand is scalded in it' — the reality is that most things do not cook when placed in a kli rishon that is removed from the fire. But there are things that do cook in it, and these are enumerated in this seif.
587: (61) 'Spices' — even spices (and not like salt mentioned in the continuation of the sentence). And in seif 10 it appears that it is forbidden even to pour from a kli rishon onto spices.
589: (62) 'Like bull's meat' — meaning: salt requires cooking like beef. That is: salt certainly does not cook in a pot removed from the fire, and therefore it is permitted to add salt to it.
591: (63) 'Of bull' — according to this view, since the salt somewhat softens the meat, the meat may cook slightly even in a kli rishon that is not on the fire.
593: (64) 'Also forbidden' — according to the Rama, the stringent view forbids placing bull's meat in a kli rishon that is on the fire even without salt, for the decree against a kli rishon on the fire is general.
595: (65) 'Because of the blood in it' — even meat that was salted and the blood removed is forbidden to place in a kli rishon, because it cooks it on Shabbos; but meat that was not salted is forbidden to place in it because of the blood.
597: (66) 'That it is yad soledes bo' — according to this view one should be concerned that salt cooks easily.
599: (67) 'May a blessing come upon him' — from the primary law it is permitted to give salt in a vessel that is not on the fire even when it is hot, and as halacha one may rely on this. However there is room to be stringent.
601: (68) 'Who transgressed a prohibition' — who transgressed the prohibition of cooking by Torah law.
603: (69) 'On top of the food' — even though food cooked on Shabbos is forbidden to eat, as we saw at the beginning of the siman, here the food itself is already cooked and can be eaten even without the added salt. Therefore cooking the salt does not retroactively render the food itself forbidden.
606: 'And if he passed and gave salt, etc.' — and regarding spices, when placed in a kli rishon even though a small amount was also given before Shabbos, one should examine b'dieved regarding the dish, for it is a davar she'yesh lo matirin. But Rabbeinu Simcha permits salt since it dissolves immediately and does not cook, for salt requires cooking etc. And it is nullified before it becomes forbidden. But regarding spices this is not so, and it is possible that here too it is nullified before it cooks — and this requires further study.
611: (10) It is forbidden to place spices in a bowl and pour from a kli rishon onto them.
614: (16) 'And to pour from a kli rishon' — for we rule like Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam that pouring from a kli rishon is treated as a kli rishon for stringency but not for leniency, such as to kasher a vessel that requires hag'alah by pouring from a kli rishon, as explained in Yoreh De'ah.
616: (32) 'It is forbidden to place, etc.' — and if he poured, the outer layer is forbidden since it was cooked on Shabbos. For Rabbeinu Tam inferred this from the Mishnah of Shabbos — see Tosafos.
618: (29) 'From a kli rishon' — and if he poured, the outer layer is forbidden since it was cooked on Shabbos. And see the Magen Avraham.
620: (35) 'Seif 10, forbidden' — from the Jerusalem Talmud there, brought by Tosafos and the Rosh, derived from what is stated in Zevachim 95 and Pesachim 76 that pouring from a kli rishon cooks the outer layer.
622: (74) 'From a kli rishon' — even though spices do not cook in a kli sheni as stated above, nevertheless pouring from a kli rishon — we rule that it cooks the outer layer. And even b'dieved it is forbidden if he poured directly onto the spices.
624: (70) 'From a kli rishon' — we learned in seif 4 that pouring from a kli rishon does not cook, except for old salted fish and kolyas ha'ispanin. The Mechaber adds here that it is also forbidden to pour from a kli rishon onto spices.
627: 'It is forbidden to place spices, etc.' — for other items besides water and oil, it is already explained above in seif 5 that one should be careful l'chatchila even in a kli sheni. But regarding b'dieved one should not be stringent in a kli sheni. And for pouring from a kli rishon, it appears their law is like spices. And all this is for something that was not roasted or baked. But for something roasted or baked one should not forbid b'dieved even if placed in a kli rishon.
632: (11) A bathtub (meaning a vessel in which one bathes) of a bathhouse that is full of hot water — {even though it is a kli sheni (Tosafos and Rosh and Tur)} — one does not add cold water to it, since it heats them greatly. But one may pour from the hot water in this bathtub into another bathtub of cold water.
635: (17) 'A bathtub of a bathhouse, etc.' — in the Tur it is written 'but a bowl of hot water, etc.' and this is very astonishing, for he ruled against the entire halacha stated in the Talmud. The Beit Yosef gave two explanations, neither of which is satisfactory.
637: (33) 'Full of hot water' — and even in the hot springs of Tiberias it is forbidden to add cold water to a bathtub that was drawn from the spring; rather one must take from the bathtub with a kli sheni and afterward give the water to the bathtub with cold water.
639: (34) 'Which is a kli sheni' — since they are for bathing, it is presumed they are heated greatly and the cold water mixed into them will cook, even though the bathtub is a kli sheni [Tur].
641: (35) 'But he gives' — and even from a kli rishon it is permitted to pour into cold water, since the lower amount overcomes the upper and cools it [Tur]. And even though it is forbidden to pour from a kli rishon onto spices, here it is different since the cold overcomes.
643: (30) 'Hot water' — and even in the hot springs of Tiberias it is forbidden to add cold water to a bathtub drawn from the spring; rather one must take from the bathtub with a kli sheni and then give the water to the cold-water bathtub.
645: (31) 'From hot water' — and even from a kli rishon it is permitted to pour into cold water, since the lower amount overcomes the upper and cools it — Tur.
647: (75) 'Full of hot water' — and even in the hot springs of Tiberias it is forbidden to add cold water to a bathtub drawn from the spring; rather one must take from the bathtub with a kli sheni and then give the water to the cold bathtub.
649: (76) 'Even though it is a kli sheni' — since they are for bathing it is presumed they are heated greatly and the cold water mixed into them will cook, even though the bathtub is a kli sheni [Tur].
651: (77) 'One does not give it cold water' — see the later authorities who wrote that specifically a small amount of water that can cook there is forbidden, but if one gives so much that the hot water becomes lukewarm, it is permitted.
653: (78) 'But he gives, etc.' — and even if the bathtub is a kli rishon it is permitted to pour into cold water if the cold water is more than the hot.
655: (79) 'Into another bathtub' — the novel point is that even though it is a bathtub we do not decree, and all the more so into another vessel that has cold water.
658: And in the Tur's statement that the reason is that the lower overcomes — it is appropriate to explain his words, since Rashi explained this reason and Tosafos rejected it in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, saying that according to the one who holds the upper overcomes, it is difficult from here.
660: 'A bathtub of a bathhouse' — and we are dealing with someone who wants to enter and take a small amount of hot water to bathe his face, hands, and feet afterward, which is permitted if they were heated before Shabbos.
662: 'But he gives, etc.' — see the Mishna Berurah regarding what is written: if they are more than the hot, that is implied from the Magen Avraham. And it appears to me that if now the hand is not scalded in them, even if they were not initially more than the hot, it is permitted.
664: 'Regarding that bathtub, etc.' — see the Mishna Berurah: the cold water should be more than the hot if the bathtub is a kli rishon; and if it was a kli sheni it is implied from the Taz that according to all it is permitted even if the cold is not more than the hot.
679: (12) A meicham from which hot water was emptied: it is permitted to put cold water {in large amounts} into it in order to warm them slightly; and it is permitted to pour from this meicham into cold water or cold water into it, as long as they are not in a kli rishon {and the water does not contain enough to be heated until the hand is scalded in it}.
682: (36) 'Large amounts' — and we do not say that combining with the vessel is a concern, for something unintended is not appropriately designated a psik reisha and made liable, since when he intends to act he performs a melacha.
684: (32) 'A large amount' — we do not say that the vessel combines, for an unintended act — it is not appropriate to say it is a psik reisha and make him liable.
686: (38) 'Seif 12, meicham that was emptied' — taking the answer of Rav Ada, for Rav and Shmuel hold like him.
688: (39) 'And it is permitted to pour' — there, Shabbos 42a, like Beit Hillel, and as the Gemara concludes: we saw Rava, etc.
690: (40) 'And as long as it is not' — inferred from what is taught: 'in what case? In a cup.' And a cup is a kli sheni, and therefore he did not explain whether hot into cold or cold, since the Gemara does not clarify it.
692: (41) 'And if the water' — the Tur and the poskim explain that placing hot water into cold water is also permitted, for he relies on what was written in seif 11 in the gloss that even though it is a kli sheni the ruling applies.
694: (80) 'Much cold water, etc.' — but a small amount of water that could be heated by the hot water until it becomes yad soledes bo is forbidden. But a large amount is permitted even if one fills it completely, since there is no psik reisha.
696: (81) 'Into cold water, or cold into it, etc.' — and in both cases even if the cold water is in small amounts and the hand is still scalded in them after mixing, it is also permitted since it is in a kli sheni.
698: (82) 'That they should not be in a kli rishon' — for if the hot water is in a kli rishon it is forbidden to pour cold water into it. And the same applies: it is forbidden to pour from it into a small amount of cold water that would reach yad soledes bo.
700: (83) 'And if the water is in large amounts' — this refers to cold into hot water, and likewise if hot water is poured into cold, it is permitted if the cold is more.
702: (84) 'As long as they remove their coldness' — and even somewhat warm, like lukewarm, is permitted, as long as the hand is not scalded in them.
704: (85) 'As long as it is not on the fire' — and the same near the fire in a place where it can cook, lest he forget and leave it there, as stated later in seif 14.
706: (76) 'Hot water' — and the meicham itself is still very hot, since it was on the fire.
708: (77) 'To warm them slightly' — to remove their coldness. And it is forbidden to pour water into it if the water will reach yad soledes bo, such as if dealing with a small amount of water, as the Rama writes.
710: (78) 'Cold water' — even from a kli rishon, since we learned that there is no power in pouring to cook water, and pouring is forbidden specifically for spices.
712: (79) 'Because it heats greatly' — meaning: it is forbidden to pour cold water into a meicham full of hot water that was boiled in it, since the cold water cooks in the hot water.
714: (80) 'On the fire' — meaning: one must not add to a kli rishon that is not on the fire only when adding a small amount of cold water to a large amount of hot water; but the reverse is permitted, since the cold overcomes.
719: (13) It is permitted to place a jug of water or other liquids in a kli sheni that has warm water in it; but in a kli rishon it is forbidden.
722: (19) 'In a kli sheni that has water' — in the Gemara in chapter Kira it states that R' told R' Shimon bar Avdimi: take it in a kli sheni and place it. And we wrote in Yoreh De'ah at the end of siman 92 that if one draws with an empty vessel from the kli rishon, that vessel has the status of a kli rishon.
724: (33) 'In a kli sheni' — and see Yoreh De'ah, I wrote in the name of the Taz that if one draws in an empty vessel from the kli rishon, that vessel has the status of a kli rishon and it is forbidden to place a jug in it.
732: (86) 'A jug of water' — even water alone without a vessel it is also permitted to mix in a kli sheni as stated in seif 12. The jug is specified because of the end of the clause, to teach us that in a kli rishon it is forbidden.
734: (87) 'In a kli sheni' — it is called a kli sheni when the hot water was poured from the kli rishon in which it was boiled into this vessel. It is permitted even when yad soledes bo. But if one draws in an empty vessel directly from the kli rishon, that vessel has the status of a kli rishon.
736: (81) 'That has hot water in it' — this seif deals with a vessel filled with water, and asks whether it is permitted to place it inside hot water in order to warm the water within it.
738: (82) 'Forbidden' — because the kli rishon also cooks the water in the jug.
741: 'But in a kli rishon it is forbidden' — it appears that if the cold water in the upper vessel is so great that it could not possibly be cooked, it is permitted, for it is no worse than the case where a vessel intervenes.
743: A food that comes as a solid piece, such as a piece of meat: some are stringent and hold that it retains heat inside, and even in a kli sheni it should be regarded as a kli rishon as long as the hand is scalded in it. And one should be stringent in this.
745: The poskim disagree about how to view the broth inside a ladle — whether as a kli rishon or kli sheni. And it appears as halacha that it is a kli sheni, but if it remained in the ladle for a lengthy time it may be treated as a kli rishon.
750: (14) It is permitted to place a small pitcher of water or other liquids opposite the fire in order to remove their chill, provided that one places it in a location where it cannot reach yad soledes bo, meaning a place where one's stomach would not be scalded by it. And the same applies to fruits. But if it is dry food that is fit to eat raw — it is forbidden even far from the fire if the hand is scalded there.
753: (37) 'Eaten as they are raw' — meaning nevertheless it is forbidden to place them close to the fire; but far from the fire, even something not eaten raw is permitted.
755: (45) 'Seif 14, but it is forbidden, etc.' — and even the Jerusalem Talmud agrees, as above. And in the Gemara according to the reading of the Geonim, we infer that its warming is not its cooking, and even so it is forbidden.
757: (46) 'And the same applies' — we learn from the above.
759: (88) 'In a matter that he cannot, etc.' — meaning even if the water and liquids were left there for a long time they would not become warm enough.
761: (89) 'Meaning a place where one's stomach, etc.' — for we cannot estimate by hand, since some people recoil from minimal heat and others do not.
763: (90) 'Since it can, etc.' — and we are concerned lest he forget to remove it.
765: (91) 'And the same applies to fruits' — meaning it is forbidden to place them in a warm place to remove their chill lest he forget until they roast.
767: (83) 'To remove their chill' — meaning to thaw them. And there is no prohibition of cooking until they reach yad soledes bo.
769: (84) 'Becomes yad soledes bo' — here the Mechaber defines what yad soledes bo means. According to the poskim this is approximately 40-45 degrees Celsius.
771: (85) 'Forbidden' — the Sages decreed not to warm water in a place where it can reach a forbidden temperature, even though the warming itself has no prohibition of cooking.
773: (86) 'To cook there' — lest he unintentionally leave the water there for the amount of time it takes to cook. And they decreed this even though it is a rabbinic prohibition, since by Torah law there is no prohibition of cooking close to a fire but not on it.
775: (87) 'As they are raw' — and cooking applies to them even though they are fit to eat without cooking, since cooking changes them significantly.
777: (88) 'Siman 254 seif 4' — where it is explained that leaving raw fruits on erev Shabbos close to a pot is easier than other foods, since as they are fit to eat raw the Sages were lenient regarding the decree of lest he come to rake.
780: 'To remove their chill' — and even to thaw them it is permitted since they cannot reach the measure of yad soledes bo [Tosafos on page 48a].
785: (15) Something that was fully cooked and is dry with no broth in it may be placed opposite the fire even in a place where the hand is scalded. {Rama: And even if it already cooled. But if it is boiling, even something that has broth in it is permitted. And some are lenient to say that anything not placed directly on the fire or stove but only close to it — even if it cooled — is permitted (Maggid Mishneh chapter 22). And the custom is to be lenient in this if it has not completely cooled, and as I wrote above in siman 253.}
788: (38) 'It is permitted to place it opposite the fire' — for it is comparable to leaving it on a stove, which is permitted; and even though nothing intervenes between it and the fire, since the Sages required moving it somewhat away from the fire there is a recognizable distinction and he will not come to rake the coals — the Rosh.
790: (39) 'If it did not cool completely, it is permitted' — for he holds there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking even in broth that cooled.
792: (40) 'If it did not cool completely' — the reason is that there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking even in broth that cooled.
794: (47) 'Seif 15, something' — we learn from oil: according to the view that holds oil has no concern of cooking; and see seif 4 and seif 8.
796: (48) 'And even, etc., but' — as written in seif 4.
798: (6) 'Cooled' — see the Beer Heitev and see Rabbeinu Yonah in the name of Mahariv Tarani in a handwritten responsum, regarding what they were accustomed in Constantinople where the maidservants would place cholent and chicken to warm inside the oven.
800: (92) 'Something that was cooked, etc.' — the reason is that since it was already cooked there is no further concern of cooking. However on the fire itself it is forbidden by rabbinic law because it appears as if he is cooking.
802: (93) 'Fully cooked and dry' — for if not fully cooked, even if it is dry and hot, there is still a concern of cooking as stated above in seif 4.
804: (94) 'Opposite the fire' — he used the expression 'opposite the fire' and not 'beside the fire' to teach that one must move somewhat away from the fire, and therefore there is no concern that he will come to rake the coals.
806: (95) 'And even if it already cooled' — to explain the Mechaber's words: he is dealing with something that cooled, and therefore he only permitted a dry item.
