810: (97) 'And some are lenient' — they disagree with the Mechaber, holding that specifically when it is dry is there no cooking after cooking; but a wet item that cooled has cooking after cooking. This opinion holds that there is no cooking after cooking at all.
812: (98) 'On top of the fire, etc.' — for if he places it directly, even though there is no Torah prohibition according to them, it is at least forbidden by rabbinic law because it appears as if he is cooking, and also lest he come to rake.
814: (99) 'If not, etc.' — even though the Mechaber holds that since it cooled somewhat from its heat and the hand is no longer scalded in it there is again a concern of cooking as written above in seif 4 — the custom is to be lenient as long as it has not completely cooled as written in siman 253.
816: (89) 'The hand is scalded in it' — since it is cooked and dry there is no Torah prohibition of cooking. And even though the Sages decreed and forbade placing it on the stove, they did not forbid placing it opposite the fire in this condition.
818: (90) 'It is permitted' — as long as the food is hot and yad soledes bo, according to all opinions there is no cooking.
820: (91) 'Just close to it' — and in that case there is no concern of appearing as a cook.
822: (92) 'Even if it cooled, it is permitted' — the Rama brings here the method of the rishonim that there is no cooking after cooking at all, even in a liquid. This opinion is very reasonable based on the Talmudic sources.
824: (93) 'If it has not completely cooled' — meaning: the Rama rules in principle like the lenient opinions, that it is permitted to heat food even if it has broth, as long as it has not completely cooled. But due to the importance of the matter the Rama writes that the custom is to be stringent.
826: (94) 'Siman 253' — at the end of seif 5, where the Rama writes that it is permitted to return a cooked pot to the fire as long as it is still warm.
829: 'And it is dry, etc., opposite the fire' — this requires investigation, for above in seif 5 he brings the opinion of the Ra'em, and see there in the Magen Avraham that according to his view the same applies that there is roasting after cooking — and how does he permit here simply [see Beit Me'ir on Orach Chayyim, and the book Maamar Mordechai also raised this difficulty].
834: (16) It is permitted to place an infanda (a type of pastry) opposite the fire in a place where the hand is scalded, even though the fat within it that was congealed returns and melts. {Rama: And all the more so a pot that has congealed sauce — when the fat melts it is no longer visible — which is permitted (Rabbeinu Yeruham part 3). And some are stringent (Ran chapter 29). And the custom is to be stringent. However in a case of need one may rely on the first opinion.}
837: (20) 'In a place where it is yad soledes bo' — the Beit Yosef brings that the Mordechai wrote like the Baal HaTerumah — which is the stringent view here — and Rabbeinu Yechiel of Paris brought proof to permit from the chapter Kira. It is still good to be careful not to place it so close to the fire that it will be yad soledes bo.
839: (21) 'And even though the fat is, etc.' — this is the opinion of the Semag: one should not forbid on account of nolad, and it is comparable to the ruling that one may not crush snow or hail as written in siman 320 seif 11, for here he does nothing with his hands but rather it melts on its own.
841: (40) 'In a place where it is yad soledes bo' — the Levush writes that it should read 'in a place where it is not yad soledes bo.' But it appears to me that here since it was already cooked and it is a dry item there is no cooking after cooking.
843: (41) 'And all the more so a pot that has, etc., which is permitted' — but nevertheless it is forbidden because of cooking for those who are stringent as written in seif 15.
845: (36) 'Yad soledes bo' — the Levush writes that where it cannot reach yad soledes bo there is no concern for cooking. But it appears to me that here since it was already cooked and is dry there is no concern of cooking.
847: (37) 'And it melts' — for he does not perform any melacha with his hands, but it melts on its own.
849: (38) 'Permitted' — but nevertheless it is forbidden for cooking purposes for those who are stringent, as written in seif 15.
851: (50) 'Seif 16, permitted' — and it is not comparable to the melting of snow and hail explained later in siman 320 seif 9 which is forbidden because of nolad, for here the fat was thick and returns to being fat, and there is no nolad.
853: (51) 'And all the more so a pot' — for even according to Rashi — because it is nolad — it is permitted, as stated there 'but he gives, etc.'
855: (52) 'And some are stringent' — this follows the view that even in the pot one should be stringent because the fat floats visibly.
857: (7) 'And some are stricter' — see the Beer Heitev and see siman 84 which disagrees with the Magen Avraham and holds that even in a place where it is yad soledes bo there is no prohibition b'dieved.
859: (100) 'Infanda, etc.' — it is a pastry mentioned in several places, a double pastry filled with pieces of fat. One places it there in order to heat it. And the reason it is permitted is since it was already cooked and it is a dry item there is no cooking after cooking.
861: (101) 'Opposite the fire' — meaning on top of some intervening vessel, otherwise it is forbidden as stated above in siman 253 seif 3 and seif 5.
863: (102) 'And even though, etc.' — this is not comparable to crushing snow and hail explained later in siman 320, which is forbidden because of nolad — producing water — whereas here it was thick fat and returns to being fat.
865: (103) 'And all the more so a pot, etc.' — for when it melts the fat mixes with the sauce and is not noticeable, and this is truly comparable to what we say 'but he gives into the cup' because it is impossible to see it.
867: (104) 'Permitted' — meaning only regarding the prohibition of nolad it does not apply here; but regarding the prohibition of cooking, here it is stricter since the sauce is a wet item, and a wet item that cooled is subject to cooking after cooking.
869: (105) 'And some are stringent' — he holds that nolad also applies here, even in a pot where the fat is mixed with the sauce.
871: (106) 'To be stringent' — but before the oven is fired up it is permitted to place the pastry, since there are those who permit even afterward; and one should not do so in the presence of an ignoramus.
873: (107) 'In a case of need, one may rely' — meaning that then even l'chatchila it is permitted, and b'dieved in all cases one should not forbid.
875: (95) 'Infanda' — like our kind of bourekas, a pastry filled with meat or cheese. The essential point for this seif is that it contains fat.
877: (96) 'In a place where the hand is scalded' — and this is how it is heated, since there is no cooking after cooking. And even though the fat within it thereby becomes liquid, here the fat was not liquid before and is not considered a broth dish.
879: (97) 'Returns and melts' — we already saw that it is not forbidden to place it opposite the fire, and they were not concerned that it appears as if he is cooking. The Mechaber's view is that one need not be concerned about creating a new substance when the fat melts.
881: (98) 'Permitted' — the Rama refers to the method of the rishonim who forbid melting on account of creating a new substance, and writes that even according to them it is permitted to melt fat in a pot that has sauce, since when it melts it mixes with the sauce and is no longer visible.
883: (99) 'And some are stringent' — because it produces the fat.
885: (100) 'The first opinion' — the Rama decides that from the primary law it is permitted, but it is good l'chatchila to be stringent. And the Mechaber was not concerned about this stringency at all.
890: (17) It is forbidden to place cold water {on the meicham,} even to thaw it, whenever the meicham is so hot that if one placed it there it would reach yad soledes bo — for it is like placing opposite the fire. {Rama: And if the meicham is not hot enough for this, it is permitted even for something not cooked at all.}
893: (108) 'It is forbidden to place it cold, etc.' — based on what the Rama concluded above in seif 15 in the gloss, this should be lenient if it was a cooked item and had not completely cooled.
895: (109) 'A lot' — we are concerned lest he forget and leave it there until it is cooked.
897: (110) 'Like placing, etc.' — meaning and as explained above in seif 14 that even to remove its chill it is forbidden if it can come to cooking.
899: (111) 'And if it is not, etc.' — and if the meicham is standing on the fire, see above in seif 8.
901: (112) 'Permitted' — even if the cold item is something that has never been cooked.
903: (101) 'The hand is scalded in it' — therefore it is forbidden to place cold water on a hot plate so that it thaws, because if it stays there for a long time it may reach yad soledes bo.
905: (102) 'Opposite the fire' — similar to the decree we saw in seif 14.
907: (103) 'Is not that hot' — the meicham is not hot enough that there is a concern that the water placed on it will reach yad soledes bo.
912: (18) The ilpas and the pot that were removed from the fire while fully boiling — if they are not fully cooked one may not stir them even with a spoon, since this is like cooking. And if they are fully cooked, even though one may not stir the pot, one may stir something that is fully cooked. But wool in a cauldron — even after it is fully colored one may not stir it because of dyeing. {Rama: And l'chatchila one should not stir even in a fully cooked item with a ladle; and the world has the practice of permitting types of legumes that are taken out with a spoon since it is impossible otherwise.}
915: (22) 'But wool, etc.' — for in this case there is dyeing. Alternatively the wool requires a lot of cooking, so wrote the Rosh.
917: (23) 'Even in a pot, etc.' — there the Mahariv wrote that one should not pour even a spoonful of water into it because it cooks, as stated in the first chapter of Shabbos regarding an upright cauldron smeared with clay.
921: (44) 'And l'chatchila, etc.' — and the world has the practice of permitting types of legumes that are taken out with a spoon since it is impossible otherwise, and they have those to rely upon — see what was written in siman 253 seif 4.
923: (40) 'Forbidden' — for in this there is the concern of dyeing.
925: (41) 'And l'chatchila, etc.' — and the world has the practice of permitting types of legumes taken out with a spoon since it is impossible otherwise, and they have those to rely upon — see siman 253.
927: (53) 'Seif 18, if not' — as written in seif 4.
929: (54) 'And if' — then there is no concern of cooking, since returning is permitted, as stated in the Tosefta above.
933: (56) 'Even though' — and so it is proven in the Jerusalem Talmud — Ran. That is why they left it unattributed in the Mishnah and Beit Hillel permits, and they did not distinguish between upright and smeared.
935: (113) 'That they were removed while fully boiling' — he specified 'removed' to teach us the novel point that even in this case it is forbidden when they are not fully cooked. And when they are fully cooked, even if standing on the fire it is permitted to stir as stated in seif 4.
937: (114) 'That is found stirring, etc.' — for stirring the pot is a real prohibition, and one who stirs is liable to a chatas according to what the Shulchan Aruch ruled above in seif 4: that in this he assists and hastens the cooking.
939: (115) 'All its consumption is permitted' — even to stir in it, since there is no cooking after cooking, as stated above in seif 4.
941: (116) 'Forbidden to stir in it' — because of dyeing, for the act of dyeing is always to stir so that it does not scorch; and through stirring the dye is absorbed into the wool more.
943: (117) 'Even in a pot, etc.' — rather, he should overturn the pot into a bowl and not take out with a spoon. And see the later authorities who say the practice is not to be stringent in this.
946: 'Even in a pot, etc.' — see the Mishna Berurah in the name of the later authorities — and they are the Taz, the Eliyah Rabbah, the Chayei Adam, and the Gra. And the later authorities conclude that b'dieved one should not forbid.
949: (104) Introduction to the seif — part of the cooking process is stirring; therefore stirring an uncooked dish that is on the fire constitutes a Torah-level prohibition of cooking. And also stirring wool in a cauldron of dye — even after the dye has been absorbed, it is forbidden to stir it on Shabbos because of the prohibition of dyeing.
951: (105) 'Because of cooking' — meaning: mixing the food hastens the cooking, and is therefore forbidden by Torah law.
953: (106) 'Permitted' — since there is no cooking after cooking. And even if it is mitzamek v'yafeh lo, meaning continued cooking improves the food.
955: (107) 'Wool into a cauldron' — meaning: when it is not a pot with food, but a pot in which wool is heated with dye so that the wool will become dyed. And to do so on Shabbos is forbidden by Torah law because of the melacha of dyeing.
957: (108) 'Forbidden to stir in it' — in the melacha of dyeing there is no permission to dye after the color has been absorbed, rather as long as the wool is in the cauldron any stirring constitutes dyeing.
959: (109) 'In any case' — even if the dish is cooked, since they fear that perhaps the food was not fully cooked. The answer is to overturn the pot into a bowl, and to take out with a spoon only for legumes since there is no other way.
963: (19) It is forbidden to apply oil and garlic on the roast while it is opposite the fire, even though the roast was already roasted before Shabbos. {Rama: And the same applies after removing it from the fire, as long as it is boiling and yad soledes bo, for it is still a kli rishon.}
966: (24) 'While it is opposite the fire' — and the same applies after removing it from the fire as long as it is boiling and yad soledes bo — it is forbidden to apply garlic to it, since it is still a kli rishon. And many do not know to be careful about this.
968: (45) 'Opposite the fire' — not specifically, for the same applies if it is boiling and yad soledes bo as written in seif 5 and seif 9, and that is also implied from the language of Rashi. And so write the poskim in Yoreh De'ah that a solid item even in a kli sheni has the concern of cooking.
970: (42) 'The fire' — and the same applies after removing it from the fire as long as it is boiling and yad soledes bo — it is forbidden to apply garlic to it since it is still a kli rishon, and so write the poskim in Yoreh De'ah siman 94.
972: (57) 'Seif 19, forbidden' — Rashi in Kiddushin 1a s.v. shadika.
974: (110) 'Oil and garlic' — which are not cooked.
976: (111) 'While opposite the fire' — and then it is very hot.
978: (112) 'The garlic and the oil' — from the heat of the roast, according to the rule we saw at the beginning of the siman, that toldos ha'or are like fire.
